item.title: Trump signals surprising approach to choosing his successor as GOP's 2028 field grows
item.description: Trump says he may not endorse in the 2028 Republican Party presidential primary
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump says he may not put his thumb on the scale when it comes to picking the Republican Party's 2028 presidential nominee.

"Probably, not necessarily," Trump said in a post-midterm election interview on CBS' "60 Minutes" when asked whether he will endorse in the primary to pick the next Republican nominee. "So I may or may not get involved... Maybe I'm better off not getting involved."

Trump for months has touted the GOP's "great bench" when asked about the likely Republican field of contenders aiming to succeed him in the White House.

The president reiterated that opinion after the GOP's drubbing in last week's midterm elections, as the party lost control of both the House and the Senate.

VANCE, CRUZ, DESANTIS DIAGNOSE GOP'S MIDTERM DISASTER AS 2028 BATTLE BEGINS

"I think we have an unbelievable bench of talent," Trump told Fox News' Bret Baier and Martha MacCallum in an Election Night interview on Fox News.. "We have a great group of talented people that I think would do a very good job."

Early jockeying by the potential contenders began the morning after Election Day, with midterm post-mortems by Vice President JD Vance, Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis grabbing plenty of headlines.

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

"There's going to be a robust field of candidates that test the waters in Iowa, New Hampshire, and South Carolina and that's exactly as it should be," Nicole Schlinger, a veteran Iowa-based Republican strategist, told Fox News Digital. "We're going to get an opportunity to see which approach to our message of where we as the Republican Party goes next is going to resonate the most with the grassroots voters who are going to show up and kick tires."

Here's a look at the list of potential GOP presidential contenders in the burgeoning race to become the party's next standard-bearer and impact which direction the party will head in a post-Trump era.

The vice president has long been viewed as the likely frontrunner for the 2028 GOP nomination and Trump's heir apparent.

But the conventional wisdom from pundits is that the shellacking the GOP took in the midterms has transformed what may have been a Vance coronation into a more competitive and crowded nomination battle.

Vance kicked off the post-midterms debate last Wednesday morning with a roughly 600-word postmortem on X, blaming the war with Iran for the ballot box setbacks, in what some pundits viewed as an early pitch to eventually claim the MAGA and America First mantle.

Even with last week's setbacks, Vance leads many of the early 2028 GOP presidential primary polls, has built a formidable fundraising network thanks in part to his role as the Republican National Committee's finance chair, and has a team of advisers and aides that would form the beginnings of a presidential campaign.

Rubio, who ran unsuccessfully for the 2016 GOP presidential nomination, is doing his best to stay far away from the 2028 spotlight.

The former senator from Florida has long been floated by Trump and by pundits as a possible White House contender, and his support in early 2028 polls has soared. But Rubio has downplayed such speculation, and dismissed reports he was considering stepping down as secretary of state to lay the groundwork for a presidential run.

Rubio, who has said a handful of times over the past year that he'd back Vance if the vice president decides to launch a White House campaign, was asked about 2028 Monday while taking questions from reporters during a stop in France.

"I don't know why you're wasting your time," Rubio said. "I'm not going to talk about 2028 any longer. I'm just not going to talk about 2028 anymore."

The conservative firebrand senator from Texas, who was runner-up to Trump in the bruising 2016 presidential primaries, has made no secret that he may run for the White House again in 2028.

In his post-Election Day assessment, Cruz described the midterms as a "blue tsunami" and warned that his party had lost touch with voters, particularly in the Lone Star State.

"2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. It was an a-- kicking," Cruz wrote. "It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election. It was a Watergate-level repudiation."

In a possible preview of the Republican primaries, Cruz has put plenty of daylight between himself and Vance over support for Israel, with Cruz spotlighting his support for the Israeli government.

Boosting Cruz if he decides to run would be his top-ranked podcast, Verdict with Ted Cruz, which has allowed the senator to build a massive grassroots network.

The term-limited conservative Florida governor, who finishes up in Tallahassee at the start of the new year, ran for the White House in 2024. He was an early frontrunner before being decisively defeated by Trump.

DeSantis held a news conference the morning after Election Day where he called the midterm election results "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans across the country."

"Let’s just be clear, that is going to hurt — not just for the next two years... That is something that can reverberate for the next decade or more," he said. "We knew it could be worse. I don't think most of us thought it would be this bad."

But DeSantis, who sat for a slew of media interviews in the wake the midterms, repeatedly highlighted that "the one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of Florida."

While in 2028 buzz about DeSantis surged since last week's election, the governor took to social media on Friday to blast a report that he was planning a 2028 run, emphasizing, "I have not reached out to anybody about running for anything. Just another pathetic attempt to garner clicks."

Pence, who ran unsuccessfully for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination, has said he has "no plans" to run for White House again in 2028.

But Pence has seen Advancing American Freedom, his policy and advocacy organization, dramatically expand over the past year.

And the Trump's first vice president told Fox News Digital earlier this year that his fight to keep the Republican Party from drifting too far from its conservative roots and principles, amid a rise of populism in the GOP and big government creep during his Trump's second administration, is "the calling of my life right now."

Last week Pence argued, "The American people have rejected our party’s shift toward economic populism, and our majorities in Congress and state legislatures and governorships across the country paid the price."

But he emphasized, "The conservative comeback starts today."

The conservative term-limited governor, who finishes out his tenure in Atlanta in two months, is also seen as a potential White House contender.

In the wake of the midterm shellacking, Kemp spelled out a GOP vision centered on the "conservative principles of our party."

"It’s time we get back to those principles in the months and years to come," the governor wrote.

Youngkin, who instantly soared to political stardom after 2021 gubernatorial victory energized Republicans a year after Trump lost the White House and the Senate in the 2020 election, has consistently downplayed talk of a 2028 presidential campaign.

Instead, Youngkin has focused on his signature issue - education - by pushing to promote school choice programs through he recently formed national policy group Empowering America's Parents.

Former New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie

Christie, who unsuccessfully ran for the 2016 and 2024 GOP nominations, is seriously mulling a third run for the White House.

"The midterms were a repudiation of the GOP and Donald Trump. It is time Republicans do the autopsy, learn the lessons, and move forward," Christie, a vocal Republican critic of the president, argued in the days after last week's election. "The Trump era is over. He has led us to the greatest losses this country has seen for a party since Richard Nixon."

Christie has said he'll decide on a presidential run in the next few months, telling Fox News Digital recently that "I think there’s a lot of flexibility on the timing."

Bacon, a former Air Force brigadier general who has at times split with Trump on foreign policy and national security issues, decided against running for re-election this year and exits Congress in two months.

Bacon has said he is open to a potential run for president in 2028 or serving in a supporting role on another Republican candidate's ticket.

Sanders, the daughter of former Arkansas Gov. Mike Huckabee, earned national attention as Trump’s White House press secretary for much of his first term

Sanders, who made history four years ago as the first woman elected Arkansas governor and last week won re-election by double digits, is increasingly seen as a potential presidential contender.

Cotton, who took a hard look at a 2024 GOP presidential run before deciding against launching a campaign, was just re-elected.

The senator, an Army veteran who served in combat in the Iraq and Afghanistan wars before becoming a rising star in Republican Party and who was on Trump's running mate short list two years ago, is also viewed as a potential White House hopeful.

Scott, a self-made multimillionaire and former two-term governor who's the wealthiest member of the Senate, also mulled a 2024 bid before running for re-election.

Midterm election campaign trail stops in Iowa and New Hampshire - the two states that lead off the Republican presidential nominating calendar - sparked speculation that Scott was considering a 2028 campaign.

Kennedy, who's up for re-election in 2028, has said he would consider a White House run instead of seeking another term in the Senate if he felt he could no longer be effective in the Senate or if he felt dissatisfied with the Republican presidential primary field.

Pompeo, a former four-term congressman from Kansas who served as CIA director and later as the top U.S. diplomat in Trump's first administration, also took a hard look at a 2024 run before passing.

Asked last year about a 2028 bid, Pompeo told Fox News Digital, "We'll see what the good Lord brings in a couple of years."

He's currently viewed by pundits as a possible contender.

The vocal Republican critic of the president who relentlessly pressed for the release of the Epstein files before losing his bid for renomination earlier this year to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein has said he's "not ruling anything in or out" when it comes to a presidential bid.

Last week Axios first reported that a group of Libertarian Party operatives and anti-Trump MAGA defectors was urging Massie to run for the White House as a third-party or Libertarian presidential candidate.

item.title: ‘Yellowstone’ star Dawn Olivieri chose Arkansas ranch life over LA to reclaim her ‘freedom’
item.description: "Yellowstone" star Dawn Olivieri reveals the career dry spell that drove her to leave LA for a 160-acre Arkansas ranch and animal sanctuary.
item.content:encoded:
"Yellowstone" alum Dawn Olivieri is opening up about the turning point that drove her to leave Los Angeles behind and build the life that she actually wanted on a ranch and animal sanctuary in rural Arkansas.

During an interview with Fox News Digital, the 45-year-old actress, who is starring in the second season of Angel Studios’ post-apocalyptic drama "Homestead: The Series," shared how she became disillusioned with Hollywood during a lull in her career after years of chasing acting success.

"I realized it wasn't giving me what my dream of what it was supposed to give me," Olivieri said.

'VAMPIRE DIARIES' STAR IAN SOMERHALDER SAYS LEAVING HOLLYWOOD FOR FARMING 'SHIFTED MY LIFE FOREVER'

"It wasn't cooperating," she continued. "I didn't have offers, just like falling out of my phone. I went through a dry spell, and I was like, ‘Wow, so this is an illusion.'"

"I kind of saw through the veil and once I saw through veil — I realized in that moment, I have to make some decisions about my life that makes me happy — [it] isn't always waiting by the phone, losing my power, waiting for someone to hire me," Olivieri recalled. "I'm like, ‘Oh, what am I doing?’"

'HOMESTEAD' STAR BAILEY CHASE SAYS CALIFORNIA VACCINE PLANS WERE 'FINAL STRAW' THAT DROVE FAMILY OUT OF LA

"I just jumped ahead," she explained. "I go, ‘If I did make all this money and was successful, what would I do with it?’ Well, I would move to the country and have horses and OK, well, I guess let me go do that. Let me, let me see what. And so I did that with nothing. Which wasn't the dream part, but in actuality, it was what was always meant to happen because I moved toward my own authenticity."

In 2022, the actress left LA and bought a 160-acre property outside Mena, Arkansas. The following year, Olivieri founded the nonprofit organization Moon Mountain Sanctuary and Rescue, which rescues and rehabilitates hundreds of horses and other animals.

'LIONESS' STAR JILL WAGNER RAISES DAUGHTERS IN TENNESSEE TOWN OF 800, WHERE HORSES AND BUGGIES STILL ROAM

During an August appearance on the "Let's Talk Local" podcast, Olivieri said she is currently living in a camper on the property while she continues to build and expand her ranch and animal sanctuary.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Olivieri reflected on the unexpected result that came from her decision to leave Hollywood and create the lifestyle she had always envisioned, explaining that giving up control of her acting career ultimately improved it.

HOLLYWOOD STAR SOUNDS ALARM OVER DISAPPEARING JOBS AS PRODUCTIONS FLEE CALIFORNIA

"I think in that moment, I became a better human being," she said. "I became a better actress for sure. I started working way more than I did when I was in LA waiting for the job, waiting for the call."

"And I moved to a land of no mirrors is what I called it," Olivieri continued.. "I went into a deep relationship with the core of my being versus what everything looked like, what I looked like."

"And I would recommend that move to anybody," she added.

Olivieri's "Homestead: The Series" co-star Charles Esten, who joined her for the interview, agreed that letting go of the pressure to land the next role can sometimes have the opposite effect in Hollywood.

"It’s not just Hollywood, it’s the whole world that — but especially Hollywood — can smell that desperation of, ‘I need this to get that,’" Esten said.

WATCH: ‘YELLOWSTONE’ STAR DAWN OLIVIERI TRADED LA FOR ARKANSAS RANCH

"The second you sort of don’t hold so tightly and you have sort of more philosophy of abundance and let it a little looser. Or another way is just give it up," he continued. "I don’t mean give it up by quit doing it, but give up the need and the desperation on it. And then they finally go, ‘Hey, you want to come do a show?’"

"Yeah, literally, that’s what happened," Olivieri replied.

Olivieri pointed out that many other actors faced a dramatic decrease in work opportunities in recent years due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the 2023 SAG-AFTRA and the Writers Guild of America (WGA) strike.

'VERONICA MARS' STAR JASON DOHRING TRADED HOLLYWOOD FOR FARMING

"But I had a very clear decision that I was willing to give up this identity of being an actress," she said. "And maybe if I had to sell farm fresh eggs on the side of the road, I would do that just to keep my freedom."

"Homestead: The Series" follows survivors living at a fortified prepper compound in the Rocky Mountains known as The Homestead after a nuclear attack on LA plunges the country into chaos. Olivieri plays Jenna Ross, the wife of Ian Ross (Neal McDonough), the wealthy prepper who established the Homestead, while Esten portrays Cain Ross, Ian's estranged brother.

After Ian is incapacitated and later dies, Jenna is pushed into a leadership role and struggles with how to protect the community while maintaining her compassionate approach toward outsiders. Meanwhile, Cain arrives at the Homestead after Ian's injury and takes a much more hardline approach to survival and leadership.

In season two, which premiered on Nov. 3, Jenna and Cain find themselves in conflict over how the compound should be run as resources dwindle.

Olivieri was part of the cast in the 2024 theatrical movie "Homestead," which introduces the story. Esten joined the cast for the first season of "Homestead: The Series," which picks up where the movie left off. The show also stars Kevin Lawson Emmanuel McCord, Jesse Hutch and Betzaida Landín.

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Olivieri and Esten shared their thoughts on why more Americans are increasingly interested in homesteading, growing their own food and moving away from big cities.

"People are thinking about it because everything else is becoming toxic in all truth," Olivieri said. "Our food system has gone toxic because of profit. Our way of life in a city has become toxic because of overpopulation potentially or, again, I really think the root of it is profit and money and commerce."

"In this state of government, being open and available is just a nicer experience," she added. "It is for me anyway."

Esten drew a contrast between Olivieri's homesteading and the gritty survivalism depicted on "Homestead: The Series."

"Dawn's homesteading that I've noticed is beautiful," he said. "Our version of homestead is very extraordinary necessity, fear-based. Plant these fences and Dawn's is the opposite of that. Dawn's very open and welcoming and saving animals that need it and welcoming other folks on."

After Olivieri embraced rural life and stopped waiting for Hollywood to call, the actress went on to land major roles in Taylor Sheridan's universe. Olivieri played Claire Dutton, the widowed sister of James Dutton (Tim McGraw), in 2021's "1883."

From 2022 to 2024, Olivieri portrayed Sarah Atwood, the corporate strategist brought in by Market Equities who becomes involved with Jamie Dutton (Wes Bentley), in "Yellowstone." She has a recurring role as CIA officer Amber Whalen on "Lioness" and most recently made a guest appearance in "The Madison."

While speaking with Fox News Digital, Olivieri weighed in on what she believes sets the prolific creator apart from others in Hollywood.

"He doesn't ask for permission to do anything," she said. "He listens to his North, his guide, and he writes textured, powerful human beings, especially women, which I find is very, very rare."

"He writes them like it's coming from inside of himself," Olivieri continued. "I've talked to him about this because he will write things for a strong woman that makes you read it on the page and then look around, like, ‘Is someone watching me? How are you in my head?’"

Olivieri recalled asking Sheridan how he was able to write female characters with such insight.

"I went to him and I said, ‘How do you know how to do that?’ And he told me point blank, he said his mom was a strong woman," she remembered. "So he had a very, very, very close example of how strong women move and what they do and how they think and the way that they talk."

"He writes things poetically," she continued. "He has texture. There's magic in the way that he writes and it's just undeniable. And he agrees he's tapped. He'll sit and wait for the muse and the muse will share the story with him. And that's how he writes."

"It's no different than all of the great writers in the sense that they are very clear that it's not quite them," Olivieri added. "They are a conduit for some energy that flows through them. And he has told me that that's exactly what happens for him."

The second season of "Homestead: The Series" is currently streaming on Angel with new episodes released weekly on Tuesdays.

item.title: PASTOR COREY BROOKS: How the welfare state broke the Black family, and how to fix it
item.description: Recently, I examined how welfare state incentives broke the Black family, and now Project H.O.O.D. fights fatherlessness on Chicago's South Side.
item.content:encoded:
Recently, I got into a disagreement with a friend of mine who told me that it was slavery and segregation that broke the Black family. I brought up Thomas Sowell and Shelby Steele. Both men are at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University, and both have made compelling cases that it was the welfare state that broke up the Black family. The evidence is there. Steele has argued that Black Americans were the first group in this nation to have a form of socialism practiced upon them by federal, state and city governments. That is quite a damning insight when you think about it.

After the civil rights victories in the 1960s, we had the Great Society and its War on Poverty, and what we saw was the shift from the pursuit of equal opportunity under the law to remedies based on race instead of the needs of individuals. When you treat a race instead of individuals, you end up with a permanent system of dependency because a race cannot lift itself up. In Steele’s view, this form of racialized socialism was rooted in White guilt — the pursuit of racial innocence by Whites — instead of Black development. This resulted in Blacks being treated not as free citizens but as a special class whose problems required permanent management by the state.

In 1960, according to U.S. Census Bureau data (Table CH-3), only 22% of Black children lived and grew up in single-parent homes. That means four out of five lived in homes with both parents. This statistic comes nearly 100 years after slavery. However, after 30 years of programs and policies of dependency, the welfare state had expanded enormously and become institutionalized. The same census data shows that the number of Black children living in single-parent homes had more than tripled. We can argue over how much of that original 22% can be traced to the legacy of slavery, but there is no argument that the astronomical increase that followed was due heavily to the welfare programs of the 1960s.

ELI STEELE: THE TERROR OF BEING CALLED RACIST IS CRUSHING FREE SPEECH IN AMERICA

What these programs and policies of dependency did was change the incentives around work, marriage and fatherhood. And no racial group, especially Blacks who held their families together for generations through racial oppression, could survive this onslaught on the basic values that any human needs to survive and thrive. I know this intimately. I work on the South Side of Chicago, where roughly 80% of households have only one parent in the home. I’ve never met stronger women than the single mothers I know. They often have no help, and they often fail to understand the role that their government has played in promoting this culture — one that makes it so hard financially to escape. 

Steele’s point about socialism practiced upon us is not abstract here. Neither is Sowell’s analysis of the incentives at play. Federal, state and city programs have for decades offered more support when a man is absent than when he is present. When you pay a woman more for having children without a husband in the home than for having one, you get more children raised without fathers. That is not a mystery. That is cause and effect. The Black family survived slavery, Jim Crow and every other form of legal oppression. It did not survive the War on Poverty’s rules. The numbers prove it.

DADS AREN’T OPTIONAL — AND AMERICA’S KIDS ARE PAYING THE BRUTAL PRICE

Fatherlessness is the root of so much of what we see on these streets. Young men without fathers grow up looking for identity, discipline and affirmation elsewhere. Gangs fill the vacuum the state helped create. Violence follows. Girls grow up without a model of what a responsible man looks like, and the cycle continues. This is the lived result of the incentives Sowell has documented for decades. And these incentives — socialist incentives — did not exist under slavery or segregation. There was no White guilt then.

I have spent years trying to be a father figure to boys who have never had one, teaching them to look someone in the eye, shake a hand, show up on time and earn what they receive. Those are not revolutionary ideas. They are the basics that two-parent homes used to provide as a matter of course, before the government decided it knew better.

CHICAGO PASTOR GATHERS HUNDREDS OF MEN TO DECLARE VIOLENCE-FREE ZONE ON SOUTH SIDE

My community center, Project H.O.O.D., exists because government programs have not fixed this, even after decades. We are in the business of helping people make the leap from a check that keeps them dependent to a paycheck that makes them independent. There’s nothing like seeing someone receive a paycheck for money they've earned.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Not only that, we train people for a life in the trades. We work with mothers who have decided that they want something better for their children. We teach young men what it means to become husbands and fathers instead of just men who have children. And we help them connect with Jesus. We do all of this from the ground up, in the neighborhood, because the people closest to the problem are also closest to the solution. 

Sowell is right that the breakdown was not inevitable and not primarily a legacy of slavery. It was the result of policies that treated people as dependents instead of as free men and women capable of building their own lives. 

The good news is that what was broken by policy and culture can be rebuilt by faith, work and personal responsibility. I have watched it happen. A mother finishes electrician training and gets a real job. A young man decides he will not abandon his child the way he was abandoned. A family chooses marriage and stability over the short-term relief of a government program.

That is the work in front of us. Not more programs that reward the very breakdown they claim to address, but a return to the values that held families together long before the welfare state arrived. God still cares about the family. He still cares about fathers. And on the South Side, we are still betting on both.

item.title: Chappelle, Jennifer Welch jokes about Kirk's murder part of pattern of leftists finding humor in violence
item.description: From Dave Chappelle's Charlie Kirk joke to several Trump assassination quips, a growing list of liberal figures have promoted political violence.
item.content:encoded:
Charlie Kirk, the conservative icon and Turning Point USA co-founder who was assassinated in 2025, has been the subject of viral jokes, particularly following last week's midterm elections, which saw Democrats score victories over Republicans.

"I've Had It" co-hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan went viral after celebrating Democratic victories and laughing uncontrollably last week at an online post that read, "We're digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again." Several of the podcast's sponsors pulled their support following pressure from Kirk's supporters, prompting Welch and Sullivan to issue a statement apologizing for their conduct and advocating for gun control. Welch later doubled down in a separate video posted Sunday.

"When we apologize for laughing at a joke on our podcast, that wasn't for you. That was for us," Welch said in response to comments made by Turning Point USA spokesman Andrew Kolvet, saying it was for someone she knew personally who was killed in an act of gun violence.

On Saturday, the two hosts apologized on Instagram. "On Thursday’s show, we laughed at a joke about Charlie Kirk. It was an insensitive joke, and we should not have laughed. We regret it, and we apologize," the statement read. "Whatever our political differences, there is nothing funny about gun violence." 

WELCH DOUBLES DOWN ON TPUSA FEUD, CALLS GROUP 'LOSERS' AFTER LAUGHING AT JOKE ABOUT KILLING CHARLIE KIRK AGAIN

Meanwhile, a video circulated of comedian Dave Chappelle performing over the weekend at Madison Square Garden, in which he told the crowd, "I feel better," while discussing Kirk's assassination. Notably, Kirk had previously condemned the "armed maniac" who attacked Chappelle onstage in 2022 and called for harsher criminal charges against the attacker.

Chappelle and Welch are among several entertainers and commentators who have joked about political violence targeting conservatives or made remarks interpreted as encouraging such violence in recent years.

CHARLAMAGNE THA GOD CALLS OUT DAVE CHAPPELLE'S KIRK COMMENTS, WOULDN'T WISH THEM 'ON MY WORST ENEMY'

The promoting of President Donald Trump's assassination began within hours of him being sworn into office in 2017. At a Woman's March rally held the day after his inauguration in Washington, D.C., music superstar Madonna told the crowd, "I have thought an awful lot about blowing up the White House."

In May 2017, liberal comedian Kathy Griffin sparked a national controversy when she posed for a photo shoot holding a prop of Trump's bloodied severed head.

That June, actor Johnny Depp alluded to President Abraham Lincoln's assassination while discussing Trump, saying "When was the last time an actor assassinated a president? I want to clarify: I’m not an actor. I lie for a living. However, it’s been a while, and maybe it’s time."

10 CELEBRITIES WHO HAVE JOKED ABOUT TRUMP'S DEATH, FROM KATHY GRIFFIN TO JIMMY KIMMEL

The jokes about Trump continued even after the assassination attempts against him in 2024. Hours after the Butler shooting that July, Kyle Gass of the band Tenacious D made a birthday wish while blowing out candles at a concert, saying, "Don't miss Trump next time."

In April 2026, "Saturday Night Live" cast member Michael Che set up a joke by noting that Trump had attended the opening night performance of "Chicago" at the Kennedy Center during "Weekend Update."

"I think that's cool that the president is going to the theater. I mean — what's the worst that could happen?" Che said with a grin, referencing Lincoln's assassination.

Late-night host Jimmy Kimmel also drew controversy earlier this year for joking that First Lady Melania Trump had "the glow of an expectant widow" days before the assassination attempt at the White House Correspondents Dinner. Kimmel later insisted the joke was referring to the age gap between her and her husband.

Others who've joked about killing Trump include George Lopez and the late Broadway actress Carole Cook.

BILL MAHER TORCHES FAR-LEFT ASSASSINATION CULTURE AFTER STRING OF HIGH-PROFILE ATTACKS

It's not just Trump and Kirk who have been the subject of violent rhetoric. Republican lawmakers have faced similar ire from prominent leftists.

Some public figures have mocked Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., who was assaulted by his neighbor in 2017 following a dispute over yard maintenance. Paul suffered six broken ribs and later underwent surgery.

Actress Bette Midler made multiple jokes at Paul's expense, writing in 2018, "Where’s Rand Paul’s neighbor when we need him?" as he debated a federal spending bill. In 2019, in response to Paul's comments about Kurdish fighters in Syria, Midler said, "I DO NOT promote violence but...Rand Paul says the Kurds are being 'ingrates' for taking their frustrations out on U.S. Troops. Which is a good reminder for us all to be more grateful for the neighbor who beat the s--- out of Rand Paul."

Midler also made a remark about stabbing Trump, writing in another post, "Maybe someone in his camp can gently give him a shiv. I mean, shove."

In 2025, progressive commentator Hasan Piker told his audience, "If you cared about Medicare fraud, or Medicaid fraud, you would kill Rick Scott," pointing to the senator's past tenure at a healthcare company that pleaded guilty to fraud. Piker later walked back the comment, suggesting Scott should face "MAX PUNISHMENT" instead. Piker also called for the murder of landlords and property owners in a separate livestream.

"Kill them! KiII those motherf—-ers and murder those motherf—-ers in the streets... Let the streets soak in their f—ing red capitalist blood," Piker said.

Earlier this month, New York University professor and podcast host Scott Galloway called SpaceX CEO Elon Musk a "traitor" and suggested he should face the same punishment as Julius and Ethel Rosenberg, after reports emerged about Musk's alleged involvement in restricting Starlink satellite internet speeds in Ukraine. The Rosenbergs were executed in 1953 after being convicted of conspiracy to commit espionage on behalf of the Soviet Union.

"We lined up the Rosenbergs against a wall. This is a traitor to the West, and he should be held to the same standards as every other traitor in the West," Galloway said. (The Rosenbergs were actually executed by electric chair at Sing Sing prison in New York.)

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

Galloway doubled down on his comments, saying on a separate podcast, "I realize this is an incendiary statement, but I’ll make it and I believe it. I think Elon Musk is a traitor to the West."

"That if this had happened in any other age where we were not obsessed with innovators and money, a much different reaction would be playing out to Elon Musk," Galloway said.

Welch told Fox News Digital on Monday that she regretted the joke but also continued to attack Turning Point USA.

"We laughed at an insensitive joke. We regret it, and we apologized. We removed the segment from the episode because we oppose gun violence in all of its forms and made a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety to put our money where our mouth is. Turning Point, the group leading the cancellation against us, mocks violence and never apologizes," Welch told Fox News Digital. 

"We still have plenty of advertisers and we aren't going anywhere," she continued. "Each and every day we will relentlessly fight for equality and justice for every American, and we enthusiastically welcome the nearly 30,000 new followers that have come to our channel in the last few days."

Fox News Digital reached out on Sunday to Chappelle’s team and Madison Square Garden for comment but did not immediately hear back.

item.title: Dem governor’s tale of combat action torn to shreds by commanding Army officer: 'Give me a break'
item.description: Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore's former Army supervisor in Afghanistan says his claims of leading paratroopers in combat are "not truthful."
item.content:encoded:
Maryland Democratic Gov. Wes Moore, widely believed to be considering a presidential run in 2028, is facing renewed scrutiny over his resume — this time from his former Army supervisor who is questioning the governor's claim that he led soldiers in combat.

In an investigative deep dive into Moore's military service, The Baltimore Sun spoke with a retired Army Lt. Col. James A. "Jamie" Gottschling, who served with Moore in Afghanistan in 2005 and 2006. What Gottschling described was Moore's patriotic service and dutiful fulfillment of his role, but exaggerations — and in some cases falsehoods — about incidents that occurred overseas.

Moore's team said that "partisan politics got in the way" and led to Gottschling's latest assessment, where he told Fox News Digital: "I wouldn't call him a soldier."

Fox News Digital spoke with Gottschling on Monday.

WES MOORE PREEMPTIVELY UNLOADS ON BALTIMORE SUN AHEAD OF EXPOSE, AS SPOX BEEFS WITH 'RIGHT WING' OWNERSHIP

He said in the interview that while Moore would occasionally leave the base, the governor never saw combat. Gottschling said he would describe Moore and himself as "combat veterans" who are "not veterans of combat."

"When you think of a veteran of combat, you think somebody that's in a foxhole, getting shot at, IED blowing up the convoy, or even more dramatically, when you think about World War II movies, Easy Company, or any of those things where it's like, those guys are getting shot," Gottschling said. "That just wasn't the environment that he was in."

"He starts talking about, you know, in his TED Talk and really struggling with reintegration into the civilian world after the deployment, I'm like, 'what is he talking about?' You know, he spent six months over there, basically in, you know, a forward base that pretty much is as safe as anywhere. You'd probably be at more risk going to an ER in any of the cities in the United States than you would be in Afghanistan, in Salerno."

Moore is widely considered a contender for the 2028 Democratic Party nominee for president.

"I just think it's disingenuous to really associate with the struggle. I mean you can have some empathy for people that might struggle with the transition, but when you come over there pretty much dip into a combat zone situation, work on the staff for six months and then come out you know saying that, you know, all this trauma that you had ... and it's like, oh, give me a break," Gottschling told Fox News Digital.

"So I think it's just him emotionalizing and capitalizing on what soldiers do. And he's not a soldier," he continued.

"He was in the Army as a reservist in a staff position in Iraq, but I wouldn't call him a soldier."

The Baltimore Sun report describes Gottschling, who then held the rank of major, as the "Army officer who supervised Moore daily" in Afghanistan. Moore has framed himself as a paratrooper in the famed 82nd Airborne Division who led troops into battle during his deployment overseas.

Moore worked on information operations coordination while the pair were stationed together at Forward Operating Base Salerno in the Khost Province near Afghanistan's border with Pakistan. According to The Baltimore Sun, Moore's job was "analyzing reports from infantry battalions and provincial reconstruction teams, coordinating for civilian assistance and helping Afghan officials communicate with the public."

Central to Moore's personal narrative is that he led troops into combat in Afghanistan. He said that on multiple occasions on X while he was campaigning for Maryland's governorship.

WES MOORE WARNS DHS FEDERAL OCCUPATION OF NEW ICE COMPOUND NOW UNDER STATE INVESTIGATION

"I’ve seen real patriotism when I led paratroopers in combat in Afghanistan and I’ve seen it in my own family," he said in a Nov. 6, 2022 post, just two days before he was elected governor.

"Service has defined my life, starting when I joined the Army when I was 17, through leading soldiers in combat with the 82nd Airborne in Afghanistan, to today," he said in a post earlier that year.

In his book, "The Work," Moore describes being shot at.

"As a soldier, you never forget the first time you were shot at," he wrote in the book. "A sudden, stunning commotion engulfs you—the sound of shells buzzing past your ears, a flurry of divots leaping out of the earth around your feet—but then your training kicks in," the book says.

"Moments before those first shots came at me, I was convinced I was prepared for the experience," the book continues.

MARYLAND'S LONE CONGRESSIONAL REPUBLICAN BLASTS MOORE'S REDISTRICTING PUSH AS ALLEGED 2028 WHITE HOUSE PLAY

Moore, who is widely considered a contender for the Democratic nominee for president in 2028, reaffirmed that that passage from his book was true during a July interview with CNN, again claiming that he "led soldiers in combat."

Gottschling also contests the extent to which Moore led other soldiers. In "The Work," Moore described fellow soldiers as "my paratroopers" and rejects Moore's framing that he was ever "leading" troops in combat.

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Moore's senior press secretary described Gottschling's motives as political.

"Five days after Marylanders re-elected Governor Moore in a historic landslide, Sinclair is back to swiftboating a veteran by recycling the exact same stories and interviews they already ran months ago," Ammar Moussa said. "Twenty years ago, before partisan politics got in the way, Lt. Col. Jamie Gottschling signed an official Army evaluation declaring Wes Moore a ‘top 1% officer’ and ‘the best lieutenant I've encountered during Operation Enduring Freedom.'"

Gottschling addressed that evaluation with The Baltimore Sun.

"There’s a lot of embellishment with that, but that’s just how the system was," he told the outlet. "You’re not trying to be deceitful about it, but you want to elevate what they did (your soldiers) … so they can get their next job or next promotion."

"Now, a longtime Donald Trump donor who has openly stated his goal is to stop Governor Moore from being in contention for the presidency is working with Sinclair to contradict his own signed military records," Moussa continued. "Governor Moore’s service in Afghanistan—including earning the Combat Action Badge and coming under rocket fire alongside fellow service members—has been independently verified by official Army records and The Baltimore Banner, which interviewed fellow service members, and no partisan swiftboat campaign will change the facts." 

The Combat Action Badge is also addressed in The Baltimore Sun's story. The story describes it as a "minor indirect rocket attack" where nobody was injured.

Moussa, citing a report in the Baltimore Banner, said a Marine named Anthony Del Signore who was attached to Moore's unit said that their convoy "took some shots" at least once. 

A New York Times exposé found in 2024 that Moore for years claimed to be the recipient of a Bronze Star when he had not been awarded one at the time. He included the Bronze Star claim on his resumé when applying for a White House fellowship in 2006. In 2024, he received the award after then-Sen. Laphonza Butler, D-Calif., urged the Army to give him one.

In a story published in July on the topic of Moore's military service, Gottschling said he doesn't want Moore to be president. At that time, Moore was running for reelection as governor.

"I care about my faith and country. I do not really care whether Moore is elected governor of Maryland, but I do care if he is in contention for the presidency," he said. "I could not live with myself if I was not vocal about the truth."

Gottschling made it clear that he wasn't putting down Moore's service, which he called exemplary, but took issue with what Moore said about his service after he came home and elevated his political profile.

Gottschling called Moore a "valued staff officer" and said he "appreciated every minute" of the work he did.

"I think there's nothing wrong with that, if it ended there, that would be it," Gottschling said. "But it didn't end there. The embellishment, the aggrandizing of his actions over there that didn't take place is the problem that I have. I'm a pursuer of the truth, you know, and I want to tell the truth."

item.title: GOP wipeout goes from bad to worse as Dems quietly score another major win with big ramifications
item.description: Democrats flipped legislative chambers in Wisconsin, Michigan, Arizona and other battleground states, creating trifectas that could reshape redistricting.
item.content:encoded:
In addition to taking control of the House of Representatives, the Senate, and the majority of governorships on Tuesday, Democrats have also assumed control of the majority of state legislatures across the country for the first time in over a decade.

Heading into the election, Republicans controlled 28 of the nation’s 49 bicameral state legislatures, compared with 18 controlled by Democrats, while three states had divided control. Democrats now control both chambers in 24 states, compared with 22 for Republicans. North Carolina and Texas have split legislatures, while races in Alaska and Georgia remain pending. Even if Republicans win the uncalled chambers in the pending states, Democrats will still control more state legislatures than Republicans.

Nebraska is included in the Republican count because its officially nonpartisan, unicameral legislature is led by a Republican majority.

Democrats scored major victories in several pivotal battleground states during the 2026 midterms, flipping legislative chambers and securing full control of state governments in places that will shape redistricting and election rules ahead of 2028. In Wisconsin, Democrats captured both the Assembly and Senate for the first time in years, pairing the wins with the governorship to create a trifecta.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE MAJORITY OF GOVERNORS’ OFFICES IN ELECTION-NIGHT SHIFT

Similar gains unfolded in Michigan, where the party flipped the House and expanded its Senate majority alongside a Democratic governor, and in Minnesota, where Democrats reclaimed the House, held the Senate, and won the governorship. Pennsylvania Democrats flipped the Senate while retaining the House, and Arizona voters handed Democrats majorities in both chambers. New Hampshire also saw Democrats flip both houses of the legislature, while the party picked up the House in Georgia, North Carolina, and Texas.

The shift gives Democrats significantly more power to shape policy across the country as state lawmakers play a central role in setting election rules, drawing congressional maps, approving budgets and advancing laws on issues ranging from abortion and guns to education and labor.

The change could also have major implications for redistricting. States will redraw congressional and legislative maps after the 2030 census, and the party controlling state government will have greater influence over how those districts are designed. Democratic control could also lead to legal battles over existing maps and efforts to alter election administration rules ahead of future presidential contests.

HOUSE DEM WHO DEFIED HAKEEM JEFFRIES SCORES UPSET WIN IN PRO-TRUMP DISTRICT

Democrats could similarly revive efforts to pass stricter gun laws, increase funding for public education and expand labor protections. Depending on the state, lawmakers could also target voting restrictions, expand access to mail-in and early voting, or change how elections are administered.

Results confirming Democratic control of the majority of state legislatures come days after the party captured control of both chambers of Congress and the majority of governorships.

Axios reports that 75% of Americans now live in a state with a Democratic governor and 53% live in a state where Democrats control the legislature and the governorship.

"In a historic victory, Democrats now hold more than half of the seats at the state legislative level nationwide," Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee President Heather Williams said in a press release. "These victories reinforce the DLCC’s national strategy to build power for Democrats all across the country. Whether competing for new majorities, breaking GOP supermajorities, or gaining seats to give Democrats more leverage to fight for their constituents, when these races have the resources they need, we can deliver wins in red, blue, and purple states alike."

Additionally, Democrats may now have the necessary votes to move forward with the National Popular Vote plan, which would bypass the Electoral College, Fox News Digital reported on Sunday.

The economy, government corruption, war in Iran and increasingly negative views of President Donald Trump's job performance created a perfect storm for Democrats, Fox News voter polling showed.

Voters cast their ballots with a bleak view of the country in their minds. Three-quarters said they felt dissatisfied or angry about how things were going, while just a quarter were satisfied or enthusiastic.

Three-quarters rated the economy negatively, a stark reversal from this point in Trump’s first term, when positive ratings outnumbered negative ones by 2-to-1, as shown in the 2018 Fox News Voter Analysis survey (66% positive, 34% negative).

item.title: Drew Rosenhaus helps Brandon Aiyuk revive career; Myles Garrett is a closer; Will Sirianni survive bye week?
item.description: Drew Rosenhaus helps Brandon Aiyuk get reinstated by the NFL, but the 49ers have zero intention of welcoming him back onto their roster now.
item.content:encoded:
Drew Rosenhaus is on the verge of saving Brandon Aiyuk's NFL career.

Rosenhaus has represented the enigmatic wide receiver only a couple of weeks and already the prolific NFL agent has moved the stagnant relationship between the player and the San Francisco 49ers toward a solution no one thought likely a month ago.

It's stunning what can happen when someone who knows what they're doing steps between two parties locked in an otherwise frosty, emotional and almost hostile relationship.

SAN FRANCISCO 49ERS COACH SHUTS DOWN REUNION TALKS AS BRANDON AIYUK SEEKS NFL REINSTATEMENT

Aiyuk had been on the Niners' reserve/left squad list since December of 2025 and during that time he did and said some really dumb things that angered the team. And the team responded in kind by basically refusing to engage with the player and portraying him as a quitter.

But with Rosenhaus now on his side, Aiyuk found himself reinstated by the NFL on Monday after he reported for a physical, according to the league's transaction wire.

The Niners have received from the NFL a two-game roster exemption to sort through their business with Aiyuk, which includes either a trade or release. The club has zero intention of welcoming Aiyuk back onto its roster.

"It means absolutely nothing to our team," coach Kyle Shanahan told reporters on Monday. 

That's fine with Rosenhaus, who got Aiyuk to meet with the Niners at the team's business offices last week, a mini-summit that lasted maybe 75 minutes and was monitored by media both on the ground and via helicopter overflight.

The scene was crazy — like much of this saga before Rosenhaus entered the picture.

It’s unclear whether Aiyuk agreed to refund some or all the past bonus money to the 49ers in exchange for his reinstatement. The Niners have reportedly wanted to get that money back or trade Aiyuk as a way of getting something for what so far has been practically nothing in the way of performance.

With Rosenhaus on his side, Aiyuk now seems likely to find his way onto a roster in the coming months after not playing an NFL game since October 2024 when he blew out multiple ligaments and the meniscus in his right knee.

That's quite a dramatic turn of events.

Myles Garrett is back for the Los Angeles Rams and he's going to be a problem.

You might say he's been a problem for the NFL because he's a two-time Defensive Player of the Year, but the point of that trade the Rams made with the Cleveland Browns in the offseason was to bring a player who could close games for them when they had a lead and the other club had to throw the football.

THE WEEK OF THE BACKUP QB IN THE NFL KICKS OFF AS SANDERS, MILTON, MINSHEW, LOCK, AND WENTZ START

The Browns didn't give Garrett the luxury of those late-game leads for much of his time with that team. The Rams, who actually have a functional offense when everyone's healthy, will provide Garrett that huge advantage.

"I am that closer," Garrett said after he delivered three sacks and a forced fumble against the Washington Commanders. "I am that closer. We don’t need to look any further. I was born that way.

"Some people got it, some people don’t. Some people have to train for it, I was born with it. I’ve only continued to own it along the way."

The same Philadelphia Eagles fan base who cheered Nick Sirianni in February of 2025 when he won the Super Bowl, booed him off the field on Sunday after a loss to the New York Giants.

There was a question on Monday whether Sirianni reacted to the treatment by offering the fans a one-finger salute.

"Absolutely not," Sirianni said. "That was a surprise to me. But absolutely not."

This is, of course, stunning.

Sirianni's Eagles have lost seven consecutive games — some because of coaching, some because of the makeup of Sirianni's staff, and some because of talent and injury-related reasons.

But the idea there are questions about whether Sirianni will last the team's current bye week two seasons after winning it all boggles the mind.

The Dallas Cowboys hope they can salvage this season and Sunday's victory over the Indianapolis Colts is supposed to be some sort of statement that might be possible.

But, no.

Not possible.

The Cowboys have a coaching problem that has failed in the discipline department – which is the reason the team is tied for second in most penalties – and on defense.

Here's a fact: The Cowboys' week after week see opposing offenses play better against them than other teams.

The last four weeks the Bucs, Packers, Eagles and Cardinals scored more points against the Cowboys than they did the very next week against whatever team they faced.

item.title: Explosive House report exposes failures it says allowed Epstein's abuse to continue for years
item.description: House Republicans uncovered alleged conflicts of interest involving federal prosecutors and failures by financial institutions that enabled Epstein's yearslong abuse.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: The House Oversight Committee released a report concluding that prosecutorial failures, preferential treatment and institutional negligence allowed Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell to continue sexually exploiting young women and girls for years.

The investigation, led by Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., raised concerns about potential conflicts of interest involving federal prosecutors, financial institutions that overlooked warning signs of sex trafficking and individuals accused of facilitating Epstein's abuse.

The report identified two former federal prosecutors whose involvement in Epstein's original investigation raised potential conflicts of interest.

Matthew Menchel, a senior federal prosecutor who recommended resolving Epstein's case through a non-prosecution agreement, previously had a romantic relationship with Lilly Ann Sanchez, who later represented Epstein.

Menchel did not recuse himself from the investigation and continued communicating and meeting with Epstein after the agreement, according to documents cited by the committee.

TODD BLANCHE SAYS 'NO CLOSED INVESTIGATIONS' IN EPSTEIN CASE, VOWS DOJ WILL PURSUE NEW SUSPECTS

Investigators also learned of an alleged photograph showing Menchel skiing with Epstein in Colorado in the early 2000s but could not verify its existence or establish that Menchel's decisions were improperly influenced. 

Menchel, however, denied ever having skied with Epstein in a statement to the Miami Herald but did not deny meeting with him after leaving the U.S. Attorney's Office. His attorneys said their correspondence concerned potential legal representation and referrals, none of which resulted in business.

His attorneys also maintained that Menchel was not responsible for the final plea agreement, which was more lenient than the arrangement he recommended. A 2020 Justice Department Office of Professional Responsibility report found that Menchel failed to disclose his relationship with Sanchez to supervisors but found no evidence of prosecutorial misconduct.

Sanchez did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Former federal prosecutor Bruce Reinhart established a private law practice while employed by the U.S. Attorney's Office and later represented Epstein associates. His practice was involved in matters related to Epstein's work-release program.

Former U.S. Attorney Alexander Acosta testified that he did not know whether Reinhart had access to information about the Epstein investigation.

Reinhart did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The committee said it urged the Justice Department to investigate further former Miami Beach Mayor Philip Levine and celebrity hairstylist Frédéric Fekkai further, following testimony from Sarah Kellen, a former Epstein assistant who alleged that Epstein and the two associates sexually abused her. 

Both Levine and Fekkai have denied the allegations in earlier statements. Levine and Fekkai did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Kellen also testified that Epstein instructed another assistant to remove computers, hard drives and other equipment from his Palm Beach residence before authorities searched the property in 2005. Investigators believed the equipment could contain evidence of sexual exploitation.

Epstein's attorney, Darren Indyke, testified that he later learned the hard drives were in the possession of private investigators. Federal investigators identified a potential lead concerning the equipment but abandoned the effort before finalizing Epstein's non-prosecution agreement.

The report also examined whether Sandy Berger, former national security advisor to President Bill Clinton, warned Epstein about the search, given that he sent Epstein an urgent message 18 days before the search. However, the committee found no evidence establishing that Berger tipped him off or that the message concerned the investigation.

CLINTON JUDGE ORDERS DOJ TO UNSEAL THE EPSTEIN FILES IT HAS BEEN KEEPING HIDDEN

The committee recommended further investigations, stronger protections for trafficking survivors and reforms to prevent similar federal law enforcement failures.

Among those recommended for further investigation was Lesley Groff, Epstein's executive assistant for nearly two decades.

Groff, who scheduled Epstein's daily massage appointments and coordinated travel and lodging for women visiting his properties, testified that she was unaware he was sexually abusing young women and girls. 

Groff continued working for Epstein after his 2008 conviction.

Groff did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. 

The committee also criticized Epstein's treatment following his 2008 conviction, arguing that his work-release privileges allowed him to continue abusing women.

Epstein served approximately 13 months of an 18-month sentence and was permitted to leave jail for up to 12 hours daily, six days a week.

His privileges included working at the Florida Science Foundation, which the committee described as a sham organization, traveling in private vehicles accompanied by paid off-duty sheriff's deputies, meeting visitors without continuous monitoring and visiting his Palm Beach residence.

Kellen and other survivors alleged that Epstein continued sexually abusing them during his work release.

The investigation also examined Epstein's relationships with prominent politicians, business executives and academic institutions, including billionaire Bill Gates and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Lutnick told the Oversight Committee in 2026 that he had "done absolutely nothing wrong." He acknowledged visiting Epstein's private island for lunch with his family in 2012, despite previously claiming he had cut ties with Epstein in 2005. Lutnick said he could not recall why his family had lunch there. Comer said Lutnick addressed the discrepancy in his opening statement.

Gates testified that Epstein requested reimbursement for expenses involving a woman with whom Gates had an affair. Gates said he refused to pay, ended his relationship with Epstein in late 2014 and was never a client of Epstein's financial businesses.

Gates and Lutnick did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment. 

The committee also identified billionaire financier Leon Black as a major source of Epstein's income following his 2008 conviction.

Black paid Epstein approximately $158 million to $170 million for purported tax and estate planning services.

EPSTEIN-LINKED BILLIONAIRE POURS $500K INTO SUPER PAC BACKING KENTUCKY DEMOCRAT: 'DIRTY EPSTEIN-CLASS MONEY'

She also testified that a May 2019 meeting with Epstein concerned potential litigation threatened by attorney Michael Avenatti, not a criminal investigation.

The report identified Del. Stacey Plaskett, D-V.I., as having exchanged text messages with Epstein during a 2019 congressional hearing, including communications about questioning a witness.

Her office said she received texts from staff, constituents and members of the public, including Epstein, whom she described as a constituent who contacted her following a widely circulated hearing exchange. The committee did not allege wrongdoing by Plaskett.

Ruemmler and Plaskett did not respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

EXCLUSIVE: OSSOFF CHALLENGED TO RETURN EPSTEIN-LINKED DONATION OR RETRACT ‘EPSTEIN CLASS’ ATTACK

Regarding Epstein's death in 2019, the committee identified serious prison security failures but did not overturn the official suicide finding.

item.title: GOP lawmaker ousts fellow Republican in gerrymandered California district
item.description: Republican Rep. Ken Calvert defeated Rep. Young Kim in a rare GOP vs. GOP battle forced by California Gov. Gavin Newsom's redistricting in the midterms.
item.content:encoded:
Gov. Gavin Newsom-signed California redistricting has scored at least a 2-for-1 consolidation of House Republicans.

Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Calif., is projected to defeat fellow Rep. Young Kim, R-Calif., in the 40th Congressional District race called Monday night, ostensibly forcing two incumbents to battle for one seat in the gerrymandered district.

"I want to congratulate Congressman Ken Calvert on his victory," Kim wrote in a statement posted to X, sharply criticizing the map that effectively drew one of them out. "I wish him the very best as he continues representing our communities. It is unfortunate that Gavin Newsom’s political redistricting scheme forced two Republican members of Congress into this race."

AMERICA SAW THE BLUE WAVE COMING — BUT DRASTICALLY UNDERESTIMATED THE EXTENT OF THE DEM TSUNAMI

All told, Democrats' redistricting and the so-called blue wave have more than cut the Republican California delegation in half, from nine seats (eight Republicans and one independent that caucuses with them) to just three or four (one race remains too close to call a week after the election).

Calvert, the longest-serving Republican in California’s House delegation, had declared victory days earlier while ballots were still being counted.

The district covers suburban communities in eastern Orange County and stretches into the Inland Empire in western Riverside County — southeast of Los Angeles.

California voters approved the Democratic-backed redistricting plan that combined portions of the two lawmakers' previous districts into a single seat, setting up the rare intraparty contest in one of the state’s remaining Republican strongholds. Kim had represented the area since 2018. Calvert's prior district, which included much of Riverside County and Palm Springs, was carved up and redistributed.

ALL THE REPUBLICAN HOUSE MEMBERS OUSTED FROM CONGRESS

Calvert is just one of three House Republicans in the state to survive thus far.

Rep. Tom McClintock, R-Calif., and Rep. Vince Fong, R-Calif., won re-election in the 5th and 20th Congressional Districts. Those are heavily Republican stretches of the Central Valley and Sierra Nevada foothills — rural agricultural and mountain country well inland, roughly between San Francisco and Los Angeles but far from both coastal metros in the western parts of the state.

Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., is clinging to a narrow lead of just 3,384 votes over Democratic challenger Tessa Lynn Hodge in California's 23rd Congressional District, a High Desert seat in San Bernardino County that was rated Solid R by the Fox News Power Rankings before the midterms.

With ballots still being counted, Obernolte holds just a 1.6-point edge — about 50.8% to 49.2% — after winning the district by more than 20 points in 2024.

BLUE WAVE NEARLY SWALLOWED SOME OF AMERICA'S REDDEST STATES AS ELECTION DATA EXPOSES GOP'S CLOSE CALLS

Four other Republicans from California are leaving Congress in January 2027.

Rep. James Gallagher, R-Calif., lost to Democrat Mike McGuire by nearly 13 points, while Rep. David Valadao, R-Calif., lost to Democrat Randy Villegas by nearly 37 points.

Rep. Darrell Issa, R-Calif., did not seek re-election and his former seat flipped to blue under the new map, with Democrat Marni von Wilpert defeating Republican Jim Desmond by nearly 20 points.

Rep. Kevin Kiley, I-Calif., who left the Republican Party to try to keep his seat as an independent, lost by more than 17 points to Democrat Richard Pan.

CALIFORNIA VOTERS DECIDE WHO WILL SUCCEED NEWSOM IN CONSEQUENTIAL GOVERNOR'S RACE

Calvert against Kim was the lone GOP vs. GOP battle left by the new map.

"As an immigrant who came to the United States in pursuit of the American Dream, serving this nation in Congress has been one of the greatest honors of my life," Kim wrote in her statement posted to X late Monday night. "It has been a privilege to give back to the community that has given me so much, and I am incredibly grateful to my family, our volunteers, supporters, and everyone who placed their trust in me throughout this campaign."

Kim said she was proud of the record built "delivering results for our communities, working to secure our country at home and abroad, strengthen our economy, and make life safer and more affordable for California families."

During the campaign, both candidates supported President Donald Trump’s agenda early on and later sought to project themselves as pragmatic conservatives.

DEM WINS TRUMP-TARGETED TEXAS DISTRICT IN REBUKE OF REPUBLICAN REDISTRICTING SHAKEUP

The race turned negative, with Kim citing ethics complaints and an FBI investigation into some of Calvert’s real estate dealings. Calvert denied the allegations and was never charged.

Calvert highlighted a campaign donation Kim received from a Chinese American businessman who has faced scrutiny over alleged foreign influence. Kim returned the contribution and said she was unaware of the claims.

"With the passage of Prop 50, Californians were sold a bill of goods, allowing Gavin Newsom and his radical allies in Sacramento an unprecedented power grab to redraw the Congressional map and silence those who disagree with his extreme policies," Calvert wrote on X a year ago.

"Gerrymandering districts because you don’t like the results of an election is politics at its absolute worst. 

"Governor Newsom pouring millions into this ballot initiative while crime goes unchecked, housing costs skyrocket, and taxes as well as gas prices remain among the highest in the nation shows he’s more interested in protecting his party’s stranglehold on the state than delivering on the issues families face. Despite the passage of Prop 50, I am determined to keep fighting for the families I represent in Congress."

Calvert’s victory leaves him as the senior Republican voice in California heading into 2027.

item.title: Noah's Ark site yields first look at charred wood fragments recovered deep below soil
item.description: Sharing their findings with Fox News Digital, the Noah's Ark Research Project has recovered wood deep beneath the Durupinar Formation, but critical lab results are pending.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: Researchers investigating a site in Turkey long believed by some to be the resting place of Noah's Ark have recovered what they describe as charred wood fragments from deep beneath the surface — and they shared exclusive photos and video of the findings with Fox News Digital.

The Noah's Ark Research Project, which involves researchers affiliated with Turkish universities, has spent the last year collecting soil samples at the Durupınar site near Mount Ararat in eastern Turkey.

Durupınar, a boat-shaped formation identified in 1959, has drawn speculation for many years over a possible connection to Noah's Ark — an assertion that geologists have resisted. 

SITE WHERE JESUS WAS CRUCIFIED AND BURIED REVEALS NEW EVIDENCE THAT BACKS BIBLICAL ACCOUNT

In a 1996 paper, geologists Lorence Gene Collins and David Franklin Fasold disputed claims that the Durupinar Formation was Noah's Ark, arguing instead that it was "a natural rock structure."

But the findings haven't deterred researchers from continuing to investigate the site.

A university-backed project is now using deep-core drilling, ground-penetrating radar and laboratory analysis to examine the formation, including newly recovered wood fragments.

The investigation has also involved radar surveys conducted by scientist Khosrow Bakhtar. The project says the scientist has reported identifying organized patterns and possible chambers and corridors beneath the roughly 515-foot-long formation.

AUTHOR DINESH D'SOUZA CHALLENGES BIBLE SKEPTICS WITH 'STARTLING' ARCHAEOLOGICAL DISCOVERIES

Researchers, meanwhile, have sent the recovered wood fragments for carbon-14 dating and species identification, while lab analysis of hundreds of soil and core samples remains underway.

The fragments have not been independently linked to Noah's Ark, and laboratory testing has yet to establish their age or origins.

Exclusive photos shared with Fox News Digital show several darkened, cracked fragments that researchers identify as charred wood, some of which appear to have visible grain patterns and growth rings.

Speaking to Fox News Digital from Turkey, archaeologist Cenker Atila, who is overseeing the investigation, said the team recovered the fragments some 30 feet beneath the surface of the Durupınar formation.

HOLY LAND DISCOVERY REVEALS ANCIENT CHARRED RELICS FROM ONE OF JERUSALEM'S DARKEST CHAPTERS

Though the laboratory results on the wood's age are not yet available, Atila said that, in his professional opinion, the fragments "are very ancient."

Atila, a professor of archaeology at Sivas Cumhuriyet University in Turkey, pointed to several features of the formation that he believes support the possibility of a connection to Noah's Ark.

"Too many coincidences have come together to be ignored," he said. "The ship-shaped formation was found in the location described in the holy books. Its dimensions are consistent with those mentioned in the holy books, and its shape resembles a ship."

Atila added, "The holy books describe Noah's Ark as having three levels, and the Durupinar formation also appears to have a three-level structure."

ARCHAEOLOGISTS MAKE UNUSUAL FIND NEAR SITE WHERE ARK OF THE COVENANT WAS ONCE KEPT

Atila said carbon content inside the formation is higher than outside it, another observation he believes supports the team's theory.

"After presenting all this evidence, I leave it to those who read these reports to decide what they believe," he said.

But Atila acknowledged that many unanswered questions remain.

"Are the corridor-like and room-like structures actually parts of a ship? Do the wood fragments really belong to the ship? Will we find any traces of human or animal remains in the soil analyses? These are all very exciting questions, and I am eagerly awaiting the results," he said.

LOST CITY TIED TO BIBLICAL EXODUS MAY HAVE FINALLY BEEN DISCOVERED IN EGYPT

The researchers believe the wood discovery could mark a breakthrough in their efforts to determine whether the Durupınar formation is the remains of Noah's Ark.

Lauren Witzke, director of marketing and fundraising for Noah's Ark Scans, told Fox News Digital that she believes the discovery proves "that this is not just a geological structure," challenging the long-held argument that the formation is natural.

Witzke said that the project marks the first time research at the Durupınar formation has been conducted with official Turkish oversight, documented chain-of-custody procedures and independent laboratory testing.

Witzke said she believes the discovery could have far-reaching religious and historical implications if ultimately linked to the biblical vessel.

ANCIENT RITUAL COMPLEX UNEARTHED AT SITE TIED TO BIBLICAL CITY IN EZEKIEL: ‘STILL HOLDS MANY SECRETS’

"We won't know until we start getting results back from the labs," she said. 

"However, with that being said, it is world shaking. It's a world-shaking discovery."

Looking ahead, Witzke said the wood samples have been sent to four laboratories in four different countries for testing, with the team hoping to pursue further excavation in 2027.

Once the results from the wood, soil and core samples are available, Atila plans to apply for additional excavation permits, she said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"We do believe that we have a very good chance to continue the research and excavate next year," Witzke said.

The team also hopes its ongoing research will help address skepticism surrounding the site's possible connection to Noah's Ark.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Witzke said the project is crowdfunded and that researchers plan to share laboratory results and other findings with the public through their website, NoahsArkScans.com, as the investigation progresses.

"We've been under a lot of scrutiny because we've been releasing the evidence as we go," she said. "As soon as it's confirmed by experts, we [will] share it with the world."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

In a previous interview with Fox News Digital, Andrew Jones, lead researcher with Noah's Ark Scans, acknowledged the team still had "a lot of work to do" before drawing conclusions about the site.

As a Christian, Jones said he believes in the biblical account but understands why some remain skeptical of the project.

"I can understand because I have friends who are atheists or agnostic, and they think that I’m looking for Santa’s house or something," he said.

"We still have the lab work to do," added Jones. 

"And I hope everyone can follow along and see what we find."

item.title: Tony Romo resurfaces on alternate 'Monday Night Football' telecast and shows he's better than Troy Aikman
item.description: Tony Romo's unpromoted Pat McAfee appearance on ESPN2 during Vikings-Bills game felt like a "Monday Night Football" audition to replace Troy Aikman.
item.content:encoded:
There is no one predicting that Tony Romo is going to replace Troy Aikman as the new Monday Night Football analyst next season, but that sure did feel like an audition on ESPN2 during the Minnesota Vikings and Buffalo Bills game.

Romo, who mutually agreed to part ways from CBS as that network's top NFL game analyst following an OWI arrest and conviction earlier this year, made a surprise appearance on the Pat McAfee alternate telecast Monday evening.

Romo, appearing in a picture-in-picture setup from a remote location, was making his first appearance on any platform since his August arrest.

And he was, well, great.

TONY ROMO AND CBS PART WAYS BUT HISTORY SUGGESTS FORMER NFL QUARTERBACK WILL ADD TO HIS CAREER COMEBACK MARK

More importantly, he was better than Aikman, who is ESPN's regular "Monday Night Football" analyst. (More on that in a minute).

First, Romo's ESPN2 appearance: It wasn't promoted. It simply just happened and it felt nostalgic, with Romo sharing from his deep reservoir of football knowledge and ability to explain it.

Romo, for example, chimed in when Bills linebacker Bradley Chubb anticipated and almost intercepted a Carson Wentz screen pass to Justin Jefferson and he made the point that offenses do safe things to win games, but that's no way to win a championship.

"It plays to the point that you're playing it safe," Romo noted. "It's almost like you're play-calling the game to make the game be safe, so it's close, because our defense can win it.

"I'm like, there are ways, there's always a way to win games. But we always got to see stuff a little better if you're gonna win the Super Bowl."

That is great insight and a major contrast to what ESPN typically get from Aikman, who often repeats what Joe Buck says – "massive call," he repeated on a Josh Allen tush push conversion – or what viewers already saw with their own eyes.

Aikman, also a former Dallas Cowboys quarterback like Romo, offered the ESPN audience that Jefferson moving before the snap was bad.

"You can't have pre-snap penalties," Aikman said, "but particularly not a wide receiver."

Deep.

We know that Aikman has had his disagreement with ESPN this year and is not signed beyond the network's Feb. 14, 2027 Super Bowl LXI broadcast.

The story he is unsigned but Buck did sign a new deal last month has led to speculation about what the Monday Night Football booth will look like next year.

So, Romo instead of Aikman?

At one point Aikman asked Buck if they should talk about Jefferson's necklace.

The ESPN cameras showed a slow motion view of Jefferson's necklaces bounding up and down in all their diamond-studded glory during pregame warmups.

"I'm guessing that's insured," Aikman said in his best jeweler's expertise. "I cannot imagine wearing that on a football field. Can't imagine wearing it period but I may try if somebody will loan me some money."

Was that a rip at Buck?

Romo, meanwhile, gave McAfee's viewers a great explanation of the troubles a quarterback faces when the Vikings defense, authored by defensive coordinator Brian Flores, is on the other side of the line of scrimmage and blitzing on almost every down.

"Josh Allen is right now in a hurricane, and you don't realize it until you go against it," Romo said. "Now, I do think that Minnesota, when they started doing all of this blitzing, they changed the game ...

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"They have seven guys up on the line there. But they're only going to rush five. Your job as a quarterback is to figure out the five that are gonna be blocked by your five offensive linemen.

"Then the sixth guy is your running back's. And then all of a sudden, you're gonna try and figure out, do I bring the tight end to block an extra guy? Are they coming or not coming? And then it's like, OK, whatever, everybody? And so all this stuff is chaotic.

"Your job as a quarterback is to say, 'What do they do most of the time?' Make the game simple."

That is a succinct explanation of what to do against a complex defense. It's what makes Romo outstanding. It's what suggests he'll be back in the booth in 2027 – maybe even on Monday Night Football.

item.title: 49ers, Raiders fans get into nasty brawl outside of Levi's Stadium as heated rivalry explodes in parking lot
item.description: Video shows fans throwing punches and getting knocked out in the Levi's Stadium parking lot after the 49ers routed the Raiders 38-17.
item.content:encoded:
Think of yourself on a "Family Feud" panel. When Richard Dawson, Louie Anderson, Steve Harvey or your game show host of choice ask you, "When is the best time to fight a stranger?" the No. 1 answer should always be, "At a sporting event."

It must be. After every NFL weekend, videos begin to trickle out on social media showing two strangers or a group of strangers wailing on each other. The bell rings after someone says something another person doesn’t like or two groups are simply wearing the wrong colored jerseys for your team.

One fight that went viral showed fans throwing punches and getting knocked out. One person folded like a lawn chair on the ground as his friends continued to brawl with each other.

At least two people were down for the count before another group broke up the melee.

The fight in the parking lot didn’t appear to be a one-off either.
